449.title: Shelach: forty years (Numbers 14:33–34)
449.hook: a year for each day of scouting; a new generation will enter
449.howItsDone: The forty years in the wilderness are read in Shelach each summer; the Talmud links the night of weeping after the scouts' report to the ninth of Av, the fast day that mourns the destruction of the Temples.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Caleb saw the same giants with a different spirit. Your line was a different spirit. Today, what the night of weeping costs.

Forty days of scouting. That's how long the trip into the land took: about the length of a long summer break. Forty days of walking hills, cutting grapes, sizing up walls. Then one bad night of fear. And the answer that comes back from God is a number that sounds almost impossible. Not forty days of delay. Forty years. Long enough for a toddler to become a grandparent. Long enough that most of the people standing in that camp, listening, will never see the land at all.
screen: `FORTY DAYS OF SCOUTING.` → `ONE NIGHT OF FEAR.` → `FORTY YEARS.`

segments.voice: Numbers fourteen. The people have cried all night that they'd rather have died in Egypt, or in the wilderness. God answers them, in a sense, with their own words. In this wilderness the generation that was counted, from twenty years old and up, will live out their lives. Forty days you scouted the land, the verse says, "for every day a year". Forty years in the wilderness, except for Caleb and Joshua. Then a line with a sting and a promise in it: your little ones, the children you said would be taken as prey, them I will bring in. The children the parents feared for become the generation that enters. Punishment, or something more? Both readings are in the tradition. The text calls it bearing their iniquity. But medieval commentators like Ibn Ezra and Maimonides add another layer. People raised as slaves, they suggest, learned to bow their heads. It takes a generation raised in freedom, in the open wilderness, eating manna, to have the courage to go up. Change on that scale doesn't happen in forty days. And the very next morning the people try anyway: we'll go up now, they say. Moses warns them that God isn't with them in it. They go, and they're beaten back. A burst of nerve can't shortcut the forty years. The Talmud adds that this night of weeping fell on the ninth of Av, which later became the saddest day of the Jewish calendar.
screen: `FOR EVERY DAY A YEAR.` · `YOUR LITTLE ONES WILL ENTER.` · `A GENERATION RAISED FREE.` · `THE NEXT MORNING'S SHORTCUT FAILS.` · then, large: `CHANGE TAKES A GENERATION.`

segments.voice: Think of a change you want that keeps not arriving, a habit, a family pattern, a community, yourself, and notice the part of you that wants it in forty days. Picture it taking years, and you still walking toward it, not giving up. What small daily thing belongs to that long road, the way manna fell every morning?
Shelach, the scouts' portion: forty days of looking, one night of fear, and forty years for a free generation to grow up.
Your line: change takes a generation. Slow is not the same as stuck. See you tomorrow.

450.title: Shelach: the fringes (Numbers 15:37–41)
450.hook: fringes on the corners of garments, to look upon and remember
450.howItsDone: Some Jews wear tzitzit daily on a four-cornered undergarment and on the tallit, the prayer shawl; at morning prayer, during the Shema, people gather the fringes and kiss them when the word tzitzit is said.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forty years in the wilderness, so a free generation could grow up. Your line was change takes a generation. Today, the last paragraph of the scouts' portion.

A string tied around a finger. A sticky note on the bathroom mirror. A hair tie on the wrong wrist so you don't forget to call your mom back. Little physical things hold on to big intentions, the kind that slide off the mind by lunchtime. The Torah has one too, and it hangs off the corners of clothes, in synagogues and on ordinary sidewalks. Watch someone at morning prayer gather a handful of white strings and press them to their lips.
screen: `A STRING AROUND A FINGER.` → `A NOTE ON THE MIRROR.` → `STRINGS ON THE CORNERS.`

segments.voice: God tells Moses: speak to the children of Israel, and have them make fringes on the corners of their garments, through all their generations, with a thread of blue on each corner fringe. The fringe is called tzitzit. And it's for this: "that ye may look upon it, and remember all the commandments of the LORD, and do them". Look, remember, do: a chain from the eye to the hands. Then the verse adds: don't go wandering after your own heart and your own eyes. The Hebrew verb there is lo taturu, don't scout around, the same verb used for the scouts. Some readers hear that echo as the reason this paragraph closes the scouts' portion. Rashi says the heart and eyes are the body's scouts: the eye sees, the heart wants, the body follows. The scouts let their eyes and fears lead them. The fringes are a counter-scout, hanging right at your side. Rashi also counts the word. The letters of tzitzit add up to six hundred; add the eight strings and five knots on each corner, and you get six hundred thirteen, the traditional number of the commandments. Tradition says the blue came from a dye made from a sea creature, and that the knowledge of making it was lost, so most tzitzit are all white; some people today use a blue they believe has been recovered. Some Jews wear tzitzit every day, under or over their shirts, and on a prayer shawl. And in traditional prayer this paragraph is said morning and evening, as the last part of the Shema.

segments.voice: Find something you can tie, a thread, a shoelace, the drawstring on your hoodie, and choose one thing you want to remember: a person to call, a promise, a way you want to treat people. Tie the knot slowly while you hold the thought, and let the knot hold the memory, so your mind doesn't have to grip it alone.
Tzitzit. The fringes: strings on the corners of a garment, to look at, remember, and do.
Your line: see and remember. A string can carry a promise. Four hundred fifty days now.

451.title: Korach: sounds fair (Numbers 16:3)
451.hook: Korach says all the congregation is holy; the words are true, the motive is not
451.howItsDone: When the portion Korach is read, Jewish teachers often pair Korach's speech with the midrash of the all-blue cloak, and use it to talk about the difference between a true claim and the reason someone is making it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tzitzit, fringes to look at, remember and do. Your line was see and remember. Hold on to those fringes; they come back today, in an argument.

A speech can be built entirely out of true sentences. Everyone deserves a voice. The people in charge have been there too long. Why should a few decide for everyone? A listener can agree with every word and still sense something off, once they notice who's speaking, and what that person would get if they won. This week's portion opens with exactly that kind of speech, delivered to Moses' face, in front of a crowd, by his own cousin. And the line at the center of it is hard to argue with.
screen: `A SPEECH MADE OF TRUE SENTENCES.` → `WHO'S SPEAKING?` → `MOSES' OWN COUSIN.`

segments.voice: Korach is a Levite, a grandson of Kohath, from the same family as Moses and Aaron. He gathers Dathan and Abiram, and two hundred fifty respected leaders, and they confront Moses and Aaron: "Ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them; wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the assembly of the LORD?" Every phrase has a source. At Sinai, God called the whole people a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. In Leviticus, holiness was spoken to the whole congregation. Korach echoes the Torah back at Moses. So what's wrong? The rabbis looked under the speech. Rashi, drawing on the midrash, says Korach was jealous: a younger cousin had been appointed leader of their clan instead of him. A midrash pictures his opening move. He dresses his followers in cloaks made entirely of blue wool and asks Moses: does a cloak that's all blue still need a blue thread in its fringes? Moses says yes. Korach's crowd laughs. He's using yesterday's commandment to make both the law and Moses look ridiculous. Then Moses answers, and exposes the motive. You Levites, he says, isn't it enough that you serve at the sanctuary? Now you want the priesthood too? He even hands Korach's words back: you take too much upon you. In the rabbis' reading, the claim was that everyone is equal. The goal was to be above.
screen: `ALL THE CONGREGATION ARE HOLY.` · `TRUE WORDS, FROM THE TORAH.` · `A CLOAK ALL OF BLUE.` · `NOW YOU WANT THE PRIESTHOOD TOO?` · then, large: `WHAT'S UNDER THE ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a disagreement you're in right now, at work, at home, online, and say your position to yourself in its best words. Then ask quietly what you'd get if you won: respect, being right, a seat you've wanted, an old score settled? Don't judge what you find; just notice whether the words and the want point the same way.
Korach. The Levite who said all the congregation is holy, true words, carried by a wish to be above them.
Your line: what's under the argument. True words can still carry a want. That's day four hundred fifty-one.

452.title: Korach: not for heaven's sake (Avot 5:17)
452.hook: the Mishnah names Korach's quarrel as the dispute not for heaven's sake
452.tomorrow: Korach: Moses falls on his face
452.howItsDone: By custom, Pirkei Avot is studied a chapter at a time on Shabbat afternoons in the weeks after Passover, and in some communities through the summer, so this teaching about arguments comes around again and again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Korach used true words to reach for power. Your line was what's under the argument.

Some arguments are over by Friday, and nobody remembers what they were about. Others are still being studied, word by word, long after everyone in them has died. The Mishnah, in the collection called Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, sorts disputes into two piles, and gives each pile one example. For the good pile, two teachers whose schools disagreed again and again. For the other pile, the rebel we met yesterday: Korach.
screen: `SOME ARGUMENTS END BY FRIDAY.` → `SOME ARE STILL STUDIED.` → `TWO PILES, TWO EXAMPLES.`

segments.voice: Here's the teaching, in paraphrase. Every dispute that is for the sake of heaven will in the end endure. Every dispute that is not for the sake of heaven will not endure. Which dispute was for the sake of heaven? The dispute of Hillel and Shammai. Which was not? The dispute of Korach and all his company. The Hebrew phrase is l'shem shamayim, for the name of heaven: an argument whose goal is the truth, not the person arguing. Hillel and Shammai each left a school of students, and the two schools argued over question after question of Jewish law. The Talmud says a heavenly voice finally declared that both schools speak the words of the living God, and that the law follows Hillel's school. The reason it gives isn't that they were cleverer. They were patient and humble, they taught the other school's view along with their own, and they even mentioned Shammai's view first. Those arguments are still printed and studied today. That's what endure means. Now look at the other half of the line. It doesn't say the dispute of Korach and Moses. It says Korach and his company. Commentators noticed. In their reading, Moses wasn't fighting for himself at all. And some add that Korach's allies each wanted something different, so a fight that's about winning ends up turning on itself. Some teachers draw a simple test from this: in an argument for heaven's sake, you'd be glad if the other side turned out right, because then the truth won.
screen: `TWO PILES OF ARGUMENTS.` · `L'SHEM SHAMAYIM: FOR HEAVEN'S SAKE.` · `HILLEL AND SHAMMAI: STILL STUDIED.` · `KORACH AND HIS COMPANY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you disagree with, about anything, large or small, and find the strongest thing they've said; put it into words as fairly as they would, maybe better. Then ask one quiet question: if they turned out to be right, could I live with that? You don't have to change your mind, only notice which pile this argument belongs in.
Korach. The rebel the Mishnah chose as its example of a dispute not for heaven's sake, set beside Hillel and Shammai, whose arguments endure.
Your line: not for heaven's sake. The arguments that last are about the truth. Day four hundred fifty-two, done.

453.title: Korach: Moses falls on his face (Numbers 16:4)
453.hook: attacked, Moses first falls on his face before answering
453.tomorrow: Korach: the man who went home
453.howItsDone: In traditional weekday prayer, a short section called tachanun is said with the head resting on the arm, and its traditional name, nefilat apayim, falling on the face, echoes the way Moses and Aaron fell on their faces in the wilderness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mishnah set Korach's quarrel beside Hillel and Shammai's, as the argument that doesn't last. Your line was not for heaven's sake.

The message arrives at 11pm. It's sharp, it's public, and half of it is unfair. Thumbs start moving before the mind catches up, and a reply sent in that moment can look very different by morning. In the Torah, Korach and two hundred and fifty leaders of the community gather against Moses and Aaron and accuse them, to their faces, of lifting themselves above everyone else. It's an attack on Moses' whole life's work. Everyone waits for his answer. Before he says a single word, he does something else.
screen: `A SHARP MESSAGE AT 11PM.` → `KORACH GATHERS AGAINST MOSES.` → `EVERYONE WAITS FOR HIS ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The verse is very short. In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "And when Moses heard it, he fell upon his face." In Hebrew, va-yipol al panav. He drops to the ground, face down, in front of the crowd. The Torah doesn't explain why, and the commentators fill the silence in different ways. Rashi, the great medieval commentator, reads it as distress: this was not the first time the people had turned on him, and Moses felt he had little left to say on their behalf. Others read it as prayer, a way of turning to God before turning to the people. Either way, notice the order. First he falls silent. Then he speaks. And when he speaks, he doesn't answer the insult. He says, in paraphrase, in the morning the Lord will show who is His. In the morning: he gives the night a chance. Rashi suggests Moses hoped that with a few hours, they might think again. Then Moses sends for two of the leading rebels, Dathan and Abiram, to talk. They refuse to come. But he tried. Moses falls on his face again and again in the book of Numbers: when the people despair after the scouts' report, and twice more during this very rebellion, pleading for the people's lives. It becomes a pattern when things fall apart. Not a weapon. A pause, with his face to the ground, before anything else.

segments.voice: Lower your eyes or close them, and bring to mind a time someone came at you with words, last week or years ago; notice how fast the answer wanted to come. Instead of answering, let your head bow a little, and let the reply wait while you breathe. If a better answer comes, keep it for later.
Korach. The rebellion that brought Moses to the ground before it brought him to his feet, falling on his face first, then answering.
Your line: fall silent first. His answer could wait until morning, and so can yours. See you tomorrow.

454.title: Korach: the man who went home (Sanhedrin 109b)
454.hook: On ben Peleth vanishes from the rebellion; the Talmud says his wife talked him out of it
454.howItsDone: The story of On ben Peleth and his wife is a well-known Talmudic teaching that is often told when the portion of Korach is read in synagogue in early summer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, attacked in front of everyone, Moses fell on his face before he said a word. Your line was fall silent first.

Read the first verse of the Korach story slowly and you'll find a roll call. Korach. Dathan and Abiram. And one more: On, the son of Peleth. He's right there at the start of the rebellion, named with the leaders. Then he's gone. When the trouble comes to its terrible end, Korach, Dathan and Abiram are all named again. On never appears again, anywhere in the Bible. Readers noticed the gap long ago. What happened to the fourth man? The Talmud has an answer, and it's a story about a kitchen-table conversation.
screen: `A ROLL CALL OF REBELS.` → `ON, THE SON OF PELETH.` → `THEN HE'S GONE.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Talmud, in tractate Sanhedrin; here it is in paraphrase. On's wife asks him a simple question: what do you get out of this? If Moses stays the leader, you're a follower. If Korach becomes the leader, you're still a follower. On admits she's right, but says he's stuck: he was in the meeting, he gave his word, they're counting on him. So she says, in effect, leave it to me. She gives him wine, he falls asleep inside the tent, and she sits at the entrance, in a way that makes the men coming to fetch him turn back. By the time he wakes, the rebellion is over, and he's alive. The Talmud reads a verse from Proverbs over the scene: every wise woman builds her house, but the foolish one tears it down with her own hands. The wise woman is On's wife. And the foolish one? The same passage says Korach's wife egged him on, feeding his resentment of Moses. Two homes, two conversations, two endings. A few things are worth noticing. The Torah itself says nothing about any of this; the Talmud is answering a silence in the text. Her argument isn't about who's right. It's about him: this fight isn't yours, and it won't give you what you think. And On's problem, but I already gave my word, is one plenty of people know. Sometimes the bravest thing is letting someone who loves you talk you down from a fight you joined too fast.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU GET OUT OF THIS?` · `SHE SITS AT THE TENT'S ENTRANCE.` · `A WISE WOMAN BUILDS HER HOUSE.` · `THE TORAH IS SILENT; THE TALMUD ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Think of the person in your life who's good at asking what you actually get out of this, a partner, a friend, a sibling, an old teacher, and picture their face. Imagine telling them about one fight you're in, or tempted to join, and let their question sit with you without defending yourself. If you're grateful for them, let yourself feel it.
Korach. The rebellion that started with four named men, and ended, the Talmud says, with one of them asleep safely at home.
Your line: she saved him. One honest question at home ended a war outside. Four hundred fifty-four days now.

455.title: Korach: the staff that blossomed (Numbers 17:16–24)
455.hook: Aaron's staff sprouts blossoms and ripe almonds overnight
455.howItsDone: The blossoming of Aaron's staff is read in synagogue as part of the portion of Korach, and later Jewish tradition counts the staff among the things kept beside the Ark.

segments.voice: Yesterday, On son of Peleth went home, because his wife asked what this fight would ever give him. Your line was she saved him.

An almond tree in winter looks dead. Gray bark, bare branches, nothing. Then one week, while the cold is still hanging on, it's covered in white and pink blossom. Hold that picture against the end of the Korach story. The ground has opened, fire has come down, and a plague has swept the camp. The people are terrified, and still muttering about who gets to serve. God's final answer to the whole rebellion is not another disaster. It's a stick of dry wood, and what happens to it overnight.
screen: `AN ALMOND TREE IN WINTER.` → `AFTER THE GROUND, THE FIRE, THE PLAGUE.` → `A STICK OF DRY WOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the test, in paraphrase. Moses takes a staff from the leader of each of the twelve tribes and writes each leader's name on his staff. On the staff of the tribe of Levi he writes Aaron's name. He lays all twelve in the Tent of Meeting overnight, and God says the staff of the one He chooses will sprout. In the morning Moses goes in, and Aaron's staff, in the words of the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, had "put forth buds, and bloomed blossoms, and bore ripe almonds." Three seasons of a tree's year in one night: bud, flower and fruit, all on a dead stick. Moses brings out the staffs, and every leader takes his own back and looks at it. Only one has changed. The Hebrew word for almond is shaked, and the prophet Jeremiah later makes a pun on it: he sees an almond branch, shaked, and God tells him He is shoked, watchful, over His word. So the almond is the wakeful tree. And Aaron's staff isn't thrown away. It's put back before the Ark and kept, as a sign for the rebellious, the text says, so that their complaints would end. The argument about who serves is settled not by the loudest voice or the strongest punishment, but by something growing. After a rebellion that started with jealousy, the last word is a living thing nobody could fake.
screen: `TWELVE STAFFS, TWELVE NAMES.` · `BUDS, BLOSSOMS, RIPE ALMONDS.` · `SHAKED: THE WATCHFUL TREE.` · `KEPT BEFORE THE ARK.`

segments.voice: Look out a window if there's one near you, or around the room, and find one living thing: a tree, a houseplant, a weed in a crack, even your own hand. Look at it as if it might change overnight. Then turn inward: is something that looked dry for a long time, a friendship, a habit, a hope, starting just barely to come back?
Korach. A rebellion that ended with a flowering stick. And this week: forty years in the wilderness, the fringes, and five days with Korach, from a fair-sounding claim to an almond in bloom.
Your line: the staff blossoms. Dry wood can still surprise you. That's day four hundred fifty-five.
